claim: SpoIIIE is a membrane-anchored DNA translocase that localizes to the septal midpoint to mediate chromosome translocation and membrane fission during Bacillus subtilis sporulation.
source: SpoIIIE is a membrane-anchored DNA translocase that localizes to the septal midpoint to mediate chromosome translocation and membrane fission during Bacillus subtilis sporulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of established knowledge about SpoIIIE function.

claim: SpoIIIE complexes contain approximately equal numbers of molecules in the mother cell and the forespore.
source: We were able to visualize SpoIIIE complexes with approximately equal numbers of molecules in the mother cell and the forespore.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by qPALM data and cell-specific degradation experiments shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Only the mother cell SpoIIIE complex is required to translocate DNA into the forespore.
source: Cell-specific protein degradation showed that only the mother cell complex is required to translocate DNA into the forespore, whereas degradation in either cell reverses membrane fission.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell-specific degradation experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Degradation of SpoIIIE in either cell reverses membrane fission.
source: Cell-specific protein degradation showed that only the mother cell complex is required to translocate DNA into the forespore, whereas degradation in either cell reverses membrane fission.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: SpoIIIE assembles a coaxially paired channel for each chromosome arm comprised of one hexamer in each cell to maintain membrane fission during DNA translocation.
source: Our data suggest that SpoIIIE assembles a coaxially paired channel for each chromosome arm comprised of one hexamer in each cell to maintain membrane fission during DNA translocation.
evidence: This model is proposed based on the integration of qPALM, cell-specific degradation, and FRAP data.

claim: SpoIIIE can operate as a bi-directional motor that exports DNA.
source: We show that SpoIIIE can operate, in principle, as a bi-directional motor that exports DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell-specific degradation experiments showing that forespore SpoIIIE can translocate DNA out of the forespore when mother cell SpoIIIE is absent.

claim: Members of the SpoIIIE/FtsK/HerA protein superfamily use the energy of ATP to translocate DNA and peptides through membrane pores.
source: The members of this superfamily use the energy of ATP to translocate DNA and peptides through membrane pores (Bath et al., 2000; Iyer et al., 2004; Tato et al., 2005; Burton and Dubnau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SpoIIIE and FtsK contain an N-terminal domain that anchors the protein to the septal membrane.
source: SpoIIIE and FtsK contain an N-terminal domain that anchors the protein to the septal membrane (Wu and Errington, 1997; Wang and Lutkenhaus, 1998; Yu et al., 1998), a poorly conserved linker domain, and a cytoplasmic motor domain with ATPase activity that is responsible for DNA translocation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The α and β subdomains form the core ATPase domain and are responsible for chromosome translocation.
source: α and β form the core ATPase domain and are responsible for chromosome translocation, while the γ subdomain regulates translocation directionality (Pease et al., 2005; Ptacin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The γ subdomain regulates translocation directionality.
source: α and β form the core ATPase domain and are responsible for chromosome translocation, while the γ subdomain regulates translocation directionality (Pease et al., 2005; Ptacin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During Bacillus subtilis sporulation, an asymmetrically-positioned septum creates two daughter cells of different size: the bigger mother cell and the smaller forespore.
source: During Bacillus subtilis sporulation, an asymmetrically-positioned septum creates two daughter cells of different size: the bigger mother cell and the smaller forespore.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B. subtilis sporulation.

claim: SpoIIIE is made before polar septation.
source: SpoIIIE is made before polar septation (Foulger and Errington, 1989) and localizes to the leading edge of the constricting septum (Fleming et al., 2010; Fiche et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SpoIIIE localizes to the leading edge of the constricting septum.
source: SpoIIIE is made before polar septation (Foulger and Errington, 1989) and localizes to the leading edge of the constricting septum (Fleming et al., 2010; Fiche et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: As the sporulation septum closes around the chromosome, SpoIIIE forms a stable focus at the septal midpoint.
source: As the sporulation septum closes around the chromosome, SpoIIIE forms a stable focus at the septal midpoint (Wu and Errington, 1997; Fleming et al., 2010), where it mediates two key events.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SpoIIIE keeps the mother cell and forespore septal membranes separated in the presence of a septum-trapped chromosome, playing an important role in septal membrane fission.
source: First, it keeps the mother cell and forespore septal membranes separated in the presence of a septum-trapped chromosome, playing an important role in septal membrane fission (Liu et al., 2006; Fleming et al., 2010) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SpoIIIE translocates the chromosome remaining in the mother cell (about 2/3 of its total length) to the forespore.
source: Second, it translocates the chromosome remaining in the mother cell (about 2/3 of its total length) to the forespore (Wu and Errington, 1994; Bath et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vectorial DNA translocation is dictated by the interaction of the γ domain with SpoIIIE recognition sequences (SRS) that are distributed in a skewed manner along the B. subtilis chromosome from the origin of replication towards the terminus.
source: This vectorial DNA translocation is dictated by the interaction of the γ domain with SpoIIIE recognition sequences (SRS) that are distributed in a skewed manner along the B. subtilis chromosome from the origin of replication towards the terminus (Figure 1) (Pease et al., 2005; Ptacin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It has been proposed that SpoIIIE exports DNA.
source: It has been proposed that SpoIIIE exports DNA (Sharp and Pogliano, 2002; Ptacin et al., 2008) and that the interaction between the γ subdomain of SpoIIIE and the SRS favors either the selective assembly of SpoIIIE in the mother cell or, equivalently, the inactivation or disassembly of motor domains in the forespore (Sharp and Pogliano, 2002; Becker and Pogliano, 2007; Ptacin et al., 2008; Fiche et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Structural studies reveal that the motor domains of B. subtilis SpoIIIE and E. coli and P. aeruginosa FtsK assemble a hexamer with a central channel large enough to accommodate one dsDNA molecule.
source: Structural studies of the motor domains of B. subtilis SpoIIIE (Cattoni et al., 2013; 2014) and of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa FtsK (Massey et al., 2006; Löwe et al., 2008) reveal that each assembles a hexamer with a central channel large enough to accommodate one dsDNA molecule.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Both arms of the circular chromosome are translocated simultaneously.
source: Cell biological studies have shown that both arms of the circular chromosome are translocated simultaneously (Burton et al., 2007), suggesting that the translocation complex is made of at least two SpoIIIE hexamers, one for each chromosome arm.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The translocation complex is made of at least two SpoIIIE hexamers, one for each chromosome arm.
source: Cell biological studies have shown that both arms of the circular chromosome are translocated simultaneously (Burton et al., 2007), suggesting that the translocation complex is made of at least two SpoIIIE hexamers, one for each chromosome arm.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both chromosome arms are translocated simultaneously.

claim: The cell-specific protein degradation system developed in this study allows degradation of specific proteins selectively in the mother cell or forespore during sporulation.
source: To investigate the organization and the cell-specific function of SpoIIIE we developed a system that allows degradation of specific proteins selectively in the mother cell or forespore during sporulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The cell-specific degradation system is based on a method developed by Griffith and Grossman (2008) in which a heterologous SsrA tag from E. coli (SsrA*) is fused to the C-terminus of target proteins.
source: Our system is based on a method developed by Griffith and Grossman (2008) in which a heterologous SsrA tag from E. coli (SsrA*) is fused to the C-terminus of target proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The SsrA* tag is recognized by B. subtilis ClpXP protease only in the presence of the cognate SspB adaptor protein from E. coli (SspBEc).
source: The SsrA* tag is recognized by B. subtilis ClpXP protease only in the presence of the cognate SspB adaptor protein from E. coli (SspBEc).
evidence: This is based on the method from Griffith and Grossman (2008).

claim: Cell-specific degradation of GyrA-GFP-SsrA* was achieved by expressing sspBEc under control of σF-dependent (PspoIIQ) or σE-dependent (PspoIID) promoters.
source: To achieve cell-specific degradation of SsrA*-tagged proteins during sporulation, we expressed sspBEc in a cell-specific manner by using promoters (PspoIIQ and PspoIID) dependent on the sigma factors σF and σE, which become active only in the forespore or in the mother cell, respectively, immediately after polar septation (Clarke et al., 1986; Rong et al., 1986; Londoño-Vallejo et al., 1997; Sharp and Pogliano, 2002) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and supported by citations.

claim: GyrA-GFP-SsrA* fluorescence decreased close to zero when sporangia entered engulfment in cells expressing sspBEc.
source: Quantification of GFP fluorescence intensity showed that the protein was lost at similar rates in the cell expressing sspBEc (forespore or mother cell) (Figure 2C,D). In both cases, the fluorescence decreased close to zero when sporangia entered engulfment, indicating that most GyrA-GFP-SsrA* was degraded at this sporulation stage (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: When SpoIIIE was degraded in either cell, more than 80% of the sporangia still contained a SpoIIIE focus.
source: When SpoIIIE was degraded in either cell, more than 80% of the sporangia still contained a SpoIIIE focus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When SpoIIIE was degraded in both cells simultaneously just 25% of sporangia retained a focus, and these were faint and present only in sporangia with flat and curved septa.
source: However, when SpoIIIE was degraded in both cells simultaneously just 25% of sporangia retained a focus, and these were faint and present only in sporangia with flat and curved septa (Figure 3A), which are at early stages of sporulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The average focus intensity of SpoIIIE-GFP was reduced by approximately 50% in sporangia with curved and engulfing septa after degradation in either cell.
source: Quantification of focus intensity after degradation in either cell showed that the average focus intensity was reduced by ∼50% in sporangia with curved and engulfing septa (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The SpoIIIE translocation complex is comprised of monomers with C-terminal motor domains (and the SsrA* tags) in the cytosol of each cell.
source: These results indicate that cell-specific degradation of SpoIIIE commences shortly after polar septation and that the SpoIIIE translocation complex is comprised of monomers with C-terminal motor domains (and the SsrA* tags) in the cytosol of each cell (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the cell-specific degradation results.

claim: Approximately half of the SpoIIIE molecules in the septal focus are in the mother cell and half in the forespore.
source: They also suggest that approximately half of the SpoIIIE molecules in the septal focus are in the mother cell and half in the forespore.
evidence: This is inferred from the ~50% reduction in focus intensity after cell-specific degradation.

claim: The distance between the forespore and mother cell membranes at the septum is just approximately 20 nm.
source: Most likely this observation reflects the fact that the distance between the forespore and mother cell membranes at the septum is just ∼20 nm (Tocheva et al., 2013), which is close to the limit of resolution via PALM (∼25 nm).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous electron cryotomography studies.

claim: In the ΔσE strain, the distance between the mother cell and forespore septal membranes is approximately 40 nm, more than twice the distance of wild type.
source: In this ΔσE strain, the distance between the mother cell and forespore septal membranes is ∼40 nm, more than twice the distance of wild type (Illing and Errington, 1991), potentially allowing resolution of the SpoIIIE subcomplexes in each cell by PALM.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 39% of septa in the ΔσE strain contained a medial SpoIIIE assembly comprised of two separate subcomplexes of molecules (dual foci).
source: Visualization of SpoIIIE-tdEOS via PALM in this strain showed that 39% of septa contained a medial SpoIIIE assembly comprised of two separate subcomplexes of molecules (hereafter called 'dual foci', Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The average distance between the centers of each focus in dual foci was 55 nm.
source: The average distance between the centers of each focus was 55 nm (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Electron cryotomography shows that before septal thinning the cytoplasmic faces of the septum are separated by approximately 40 nm.
source: Electron cryotomography shows that before septal thinning the cytoplasmic faces of the septum are separated by ∼40 nm (Tocheva et al., 2013), suggesting that the centers of each resolved subcomplexes of SpoIIIE lie in separate cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous electron cryotomography studies.

claim: Dual foci were observed in 26% of sporangia when septal thinning was blocked by the absence of the SpoIID, SpoIIM and SpoIIP proteins.
source: Dual foci were also observed in 26% of sporangia when septal thinning was blocked by the absence of the SpoIID, SpoIIM and SpoIIP proteins that degrade septal peptidoglycan (Figure 4B,D) (Pogliano et al., 1999; Abanes De Mello et al., 2002; Chastanet and Losick, 2007; Gutierrez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and supported by citations.

claim: The width perpendicular to the septum of single foci (94 nm) was approximately 1.7× larger than that of each individually resolved cluster in dual foci (54 nm).
source: On average, the width perpendicular to the septum of the single foci (94 nm) was ∼1.7× larger than that of each individually resolved cluster in dual foci (54 nm), while their width parallel to the septum was similar (∼80 nm, Figure 5C), suggesting that single foci are unresolved dual foci.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PALM images of SpoIIIE-Dendra2 showed a larger (83%) number of septa with a single focus than SpoIIIE-tdEOS.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, PALM images of SpoIIIE-Dendra2 showed a larger (83%) number of septa with a single focus than SpoIIIE-tdEOS (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), as expected for a dimmer fluorescent protein with reduced localization accuracy (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and supported by citation.

claim: The translocation-deficient SpoIIIE ATPase mutant (G467S) showed dual foci in 23% of septa in ΔσE background.
source: First, we examined PALM images of the translocation-deficient SpoIIIE ATPase mutant (G467S; hereafter SpoIIIEATP−) in ΔσE background. This strain showed dual foci in 23% of septa (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), suggesting that dual foci represent the structure of SpoIIIE when it assembles around the trapped chromosome, not after DNA translocation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: 81% of sporangia with dual foci had not completed DNA translocation.
source: Quantification of the forespore DNA relative to the total (mother cell plus forespore), demonstrated that 81% of sporangia with dual foci had not completed DNA translocation (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: qPALM detected, on average, 34 ± 17 molecules in the entire dual foci.
source: We detected, on average, 34 ± 17 molecules in the entire dual foci, consistent with the number of molecules of wild type SpoIIIE and SpoIIIEATP− in strains with thin septa (Figure 5D, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Table 1.

claim: qPALM detected 19 ± 11 molecules in the mother cell-proximal subcomplex and 15 ± 8 molecules in the forespore-proximal subcomplex from dual foci.
source: We detected 19 ± 11 and 15 ± 8 molecules in the mother cell- and forespore-proximal subcomplexes from dual foci, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Table 1.

claim: Each subcomplex contains approximately half the number of SpoIIIE molecules detected in the entire dual focus.
source: Thus each subcomplex contains approximately half the number of SpoIIIE molecules detected in the entire dual focus, consistent with our quantification of the fluorescence intensity after cell-specific degradation of SpoIIIE-GFP (Figure 3B, Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the qPALM data and consistent with cell-specific degradation results.

claim: The SpoIIIE translocation complex consists of two complexes containing equivalent numbers of SpoIIIE molecules, one in the mother cell and one in the forespore.
source: Together these results suggest that the SpoIIIE translocation complex consist of two complexes containing equivalent numbers of SpoIIIE molecules, one in the mother cell and one in the forespore.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined qPALM and cell-specific degradation data.

claim: Fluorescence did not recover in FRAP experiments when SpoIIIE was not degraded, indicating that the membranes are separated.
source: Fluorescence did not recover when SpoIIIE was not degraded, indicating that the membranes are separated (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Fluorescence completely recovered in most sporangia within 60 s when SpoIIIE was degraded in the mother cell, the forespore or both.
source: However, fluorescence completely recovered in most sporangia within 60 s when SpoIIIE was degraded in the mother cell, the forespore or both (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: SpoIIIE subcomplexes in both cells are required for septal membrane fission.
source: These results indicate that SpoIIIE subcomplexes in both cells are required for septal membrane fission, supporting the model that assembly of a paired channel contributes to membrane fission (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP experiments showing membrane continuity after degradation in either cell.

claim: Membrane fission is reversible during DNA translocation and depends on the integrity of the paired channel.
source: Furthermore, the observation that the separated membranes before degradation were converted to continuous membranes after degradation suggests that membrane fission is reversible during DNA translocation and depends on the integrity of the paired channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP experiments.

claim: When SpoIIIE was degraded in the forespore, most sporangia completed chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 38%).
source: Similarly, when SpoIIIE was degraded in the forespore, most sporangia completed chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 38%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 26% of sporangia showed a normalized DAPI intensity <30% when SpoIIIE was degraded in the forespore.
source: However, 26% of sporangia showed a normalized DAPI intensity <30% (Figure 7B), suggesting that in some sporangia the absence of the forespore complex impaired the ability of the mother cell complex to translocate DNA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Degradation of SpoIIIE in the mother cell blocked chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 20%) in most sporangia.
source: In contrast, degradation of SpoIIIE in the mother cell blocked chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 20%) in most sporangia and 20% of sporangia showed anucleate forespores (Figure 7A,B), indicating that in the absence of the SpoIIIE mother cell subcomplex, the forespore subcomplex can ultimately translocate the chromosome in the reverse direction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 20% of sporangia showed anucleate forespores when SpoIIIE was degraded in the mother cell.
source: In contrast, degradation of SpoIIIE in the mother cell blocked chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 20%) in most sporangia and 20% of sporangia showed anucleate forespores (Figure 7A,B), indicating that in the absence of the SpoIIIE mother cell subcomplex, the forespore subcomplex can ultimately translocate the chromosome in the reverse direction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: In the absence of the SpoIIIE mother cell subcomplex, the forespore subcomplex can translocate the chromosome in the reverse direction.
source: In contrast, degradation of SpoIIIE in the mother cell blocked chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 20%) in most sporangia and 20% of sporangia showed anucleate forespores (Figure 7A,B), indicating that in the absence of the SpoIIIE mother cell subcomplex, the forespore subcomplex can ultimately translocate the chromosome in the reverse direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of anucleate forespores after mother cell SpoIIIE degradation.

claim: Degradation in both cells blocked chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 21%) and generated 6% anucleate forespores.
source: As expected, degradation in both cells blocked chromosome translocation (normalized DAPI intensity, 21%) and generated 6% anucleate forespores, less than when SpoIIIE was degraded only in the mother cell (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SpoIIIE functions as a DNA exporter.
source: These results support the notion that SpoIIIE functions as a DNA exporter (Sharp and Pogliano, 2002), and that although it normally operates in the mother cell, it is capable of operating in the forespore in the absence of the mother cell subcomplex (Figure 7C), generating anucleate forespores.
evidence: This is supported by the cell-specific degradation results and citation to previous work.

claim: The forespore subcomplex is necessary for maximal DNA translocation efficiency.
source: Surprisingly, our results also provide evidence that the forespore subcomplex is necessary for maximal DNA translocation efficiency, a result confirmed by quantifying the frequency with which a CFP reporter of forespore gene expression that was positioned near the terminus entered the forespore (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: SpoIIIE forms a complex with approximately equal numbers of molecules in the mother cell and the forespore, enough to assemble at least two hexamers in each cell.
source: We show that SpoIIIE forms a complex with approximately equal numbers of molecules in the mother cell and the forespore, enough to assemble at least two hexamers in each cell.
evidence: This is based on qPALM data showing ~31 molecules total, with ~19 in mother cell and ~15 in forespore.

claim: Both the forespore and mother cell SpoIIIE subcomplexes are required to maintain septal membrane fission during DNA translocation.
source: Both the forespore and mother cell SpoIIIE subcomplexes are required to maintain septal membrane fission during DNA translocation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing membrane continuity after degradation in either cell.

claim: Only the mother cell SpoIIIE is essential for chromosome translocation into the forespore.
source: However, only the mother cell SpoIIIE is essential for chromosome translocation into the forespore.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell-specific degradation experiments showing DNA translocation continues when forespore SpoIIIE is degraded but not when mother cell SpoIIIE is degraded.

claim: In the absence of the mother cell protein, forespore SpoIIIE translocates the chromosome out of the forespore.
source: In the absence of the mother cell protein, forespore SpoIIIE translocates the chromosome out of the forespore, indicating that SpoIIIE exports DNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the observation of anucleate forespores after mother cell SpoIIIE degradation.

claim: The results are consistent with the paired channel model in which SpoIIIE assembles a DNA-conducting channel that spans the mother cell and forespore septal membranes.
source: Together our results are consistent with the paired channel model in which SpoIIIE assembles a DNA-conducting channel that spans the mother cell and forespore septal membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of qPALM, cell-specific degradation, and FRAP experiments.

claim: The distance between the clusters in each cell was found to be 55 nm, which is larger than the 40 nm width of the septum in the strains used.
source: The distance between the clusters in each cell was found to be 55 nm, which is larger than the 40 nm width of the septum in the strains used here, providing some support for a channel architecture in which the motor domains of each complex are within the cytoplasm of the respective daughter cell (Figure 8B, left) rather than within the septum (Figure 8B, right), although further experiments are required to address this point.
evidence: This is based on PALM measurements and comparison to known septal thickness.

claim: The SpoIIIE complex contains 31 (±18) SpoIIIE molecules, enough to form at least two dodecameric channels, one for each chromosome arm (24 molecules in total).
source: Nevertheless, it is tantalizing to note that our counting method (Lee et al., 2012) indicated that the SpoIIIE complex contains 31 (±18) SpoIIIE molecules, enough to form at least two dodecameric channels, one for each chromosome arm (24 molecules in total, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on qPALM counting data.

claim: A more detailed analysis of qPALM data revealed the existence of two populations of sporangia with different numbers of SpoIIIE monomers at the septum (approximately 25 and approximately 50).
source: Furthermore, a more detailed analysis of qPALM data revealed the existence of two populations of sporangia with different numbers of SpoIIIE monomers at the septum (∼25 and ∼50; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting that some translocation complexes have enough molecules to assemble two channels while others could assemble four (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: SpoIIIE organizes around an even number of DNA arms (two or four) during sporulation.
source: Therefore, we speculate that SpoIIIE organizes around an even number of DNA arms (two or four) during sporulation (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), as would be expected if a circular chromosome crossed the septum one or two times, respectively.
evidence: This is speculated based on the two populations of SpoIIIE molecule counts.

claim: Septal membrane fission is reversible in the presence of trapped DNA.
source: Our results demonstrate that SpoIIIE is required in both cells to maintain separate septal membranes during DNA translocation and that septal membrane fission is reversible in the presence of trapped DNA (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments showing membrane continuity after SpoIIIE degradation.

claim: Transmembrane domains in each cell assemble a structure that excludes lipids and blocks membrane diffusion between the two cells.
source: The simplest explanation for this finding is that transmembrane domains in each cell assemble a structure that excludes lipids and blocks membrane diffusion between the two cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP results showing membrane continuity after degradation.

claim: During assembly of a translocation complex, SpoIIIE membrane domains in the mother cell and the forespore dock via their extracellular domains and the membrane domains of each subunit—within each bilayer—compact into their hexameric form, excluding lipids to form a paired central channel.
source: This scenario could occur if during assembly of a translocation complex, SpoIIIE membrane domains in the mother cell and the forespore dock via their extracellular domains and the membrane domains of each subunit—within each bilayer—compact into their hexameric form, excluding lipids to form a paired central channel (Almers, 2001; Peters et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2006; Fleming et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The paired channel model for septal membrane fission is supported by previous demonstration that septal membrane fission depends on the SpoIIIE transmembrane domain and its large extracellular loop and on the assembly of a compact focus.
source: In addition to the data presented here, the paired channel model for septal membrane fission is supported by our previous demonstration that septal membrane fission depends on the SpoIIIE transmembrane domain (Sharp and Pogliano, 2003) and its large extracellular loop (Liu et al., 2006) and on the assembly of a compact focus (Fleming et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Chromosome translocation happens most efficiently when both complexes are present.
source: However, our cell-specific degradation data show that chromosome translocation happens most efficiently when both complexes are present (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 3), suggesting that rather than a competition, there is a potentiation between the two hexamers of a channel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The hexamers within a dodecameric channel should be considered as an integral entity.
source: We therefore propose that the hexamers within a dodecameric channel should be considered as an integral entity (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is proposed based on the observation that both complexes contribute to translocation efficiency.

claim: Docking of the transmembrane domains of hexamers in opposite septal membranes might stabilize the translocation complex, distributing the tension produced by the movement of the chromosome between the two septal membranes and insulating the DNA from interactions with the membrane or periplasm.
source: In this model, docking of the transmembrane domains of hexamers in opposite septal membranes might contribute to the robustness of chromosome translocation in two ways. First, it might stabilize the translocation complex, distributing the tension produced by the movement of the chromosome between the two septal membranes and insulating the DNA from interactions with the membrane or periplasm.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the paired channel model.

claim: Docking of transmembrane domains might facilitate the deactivation of the forespore motor domains after activation of the mother cell motor domains by encountering SRSs in the permissive orientation.
source: Second, it might facilitate the deactivation of the forespore motor domains after activation of the mother cell motor domains by encountering SRSs in the permissive orientation (Besprozvannaya et al., 2013; Cattoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: A paired channel similar to the one described for SpoIIIE could function as a bidirectional translocation machinery guided by SRS-like sequences in other members of the SpoIIIE/FtsK/HerA superfamily.
source: Since the trapped chromosome can belong to either daughter cell, a paired channel similar to the one described here could function as a bidirectional translocation machinery guided by SRS-like sequences that would allow the transport of the chromosome to the appropriate compartment.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings for SpoIIIE.

claim: By analogy to SpoIIIE, the transmembrane domain of FtsK and possibly HerA might also form a paired channel crossing both septal membranes.
source: So, by analogy to SpoIIIE, we hypothesize that the transmembrane domain of these proteins might also form a paired channel crossing both septal membranes.
evidence: This is hypothesized based on analogy to SpoIIIE findings.

claim: The ΔσE strain does not initiate engulfment or block the second potential division septum, producing a high number of disporic sporangia without impairing DNA translocation.
source: As expected (Pogliano et al., 1999), this strain did not initiate engulfment or block the second potential division septum, producing a high number of disporic sporangia (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) without impairing DNA translocation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 4—figure supplement 2, and supported by citation.

claim: Expression of sspBEc in strains in which SpoIIIE was not tagged with SsrA* did not show any defect in chromosome translocation.
source: Expresison of sspBEc in strains in which SpoIIIE was not tagged with SsrA* did not show any defect in chromosome translocation, indicating that the observed phenotypes are indeed due to the degradation of SpoIIIE molecules (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.
